utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could the case be called.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-82-T, The Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We commence today the final submissions of the three parties on this trial. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned colleagues. Your Honours, before we begin our formal submissions today, the Prosecution would like to take a moment to express its gratitude to, first of all, the interpreters and other members of CLSS who have laboured to ensure that the courtroom interpretation and the translation of documents in this case have been accurate and comprehensive. We would like also express our appreciation to the legal officers of the Trial Chamber, who have skillfully and patiently assisted both the Prosecution and the Defence to ensure that the trial proceeded as smoothly as possible; to the registry officers, in particular Ms. Guduric, without whom it would have been impossible to view, create, and record the thousands of exhibits that have become part of the record of there trial. And, finally, Your Honour, we would like to express our appreciation to our long-suffering court reporter, Miss Ogston, who has done a wonderful job recording the transcript of these proceedings and who has patiently tolerated attorneys, like myself, who spoke too fast, too softly, and sometimes not very clearly. To all, the Prosecution expresses its sincere appreciation for the work they have done during the length of this trial. Your Honour, I will take a moment to explain the order and structure of the Prosecution's submissions today. The Prosecution has divided its oral submissions into five parts. First, Mr. Dobbyn will commence with submissions about the pattern of crimes that occurred in Ljuboten and Skopje from the 12 to 14th of August, 2001. Then, Ms. Valabhji will discuss the evidence of the criminal responsibility of Mr. Tarculovski, pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. I will follow Ms. Valabhji, and I will make submissions about the evidence of the criminal responsibility of Mr. Boskoski, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. Ms. Regue will discuss the evidence proving that an armed conflict existed in Macedonia from January through September 2001. And, finally, Mr. Dobbyn will make submissions concerning the appropriate sentences for the accused, should the Trial Chamber find one or both of them guilty. Your Honours, in order to maintain the integrity of evidence provided in private or closed session, or exhibits admitted under seal, the Prosecution will occasionally request that the proceedings move into private session. In order to remain in public session as much as possible, the Prosecution may refer to pages of the transcript, without mentioning the name of the witness who gave that testimony. Now, with your leave, I will give the floor to Mr. Dobbyn first, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. As Mr. Saxon has explained, I will be speaking about the pattern of crimes committed in Ljuboten from the 10th to the 12th of August 2001, and I will be happy to respond to any questions that the Trial Chamber may have either during my submissions or when I'm finished. As a preliminary matter, the Prosecution has prepared an annotated panoramic photograph which, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, we will seek to use as a visual aid during our submissions. We will not be seeking to tender the photograph, nor will we be asking that it be given any evidentiary value. It is simply as an aid to our to save time and for the sake of clarity. It has been provided to the Defence, and I hope there will be no objection to the use of this photograph. Your Honours, the evidence establishing the pattern of crimes is discussed in detail in the Prosecution's final brief. I don't intend to repeat much of what is in the final brief. I will simply touch on some pertinent facts, and I will use the remainder of my time to address arguments that have been made by the Defence counsel in their respective final briefs. Now, at this point, I would like to call up the panoramic photograph that we have prepared, which has ERN N005-8308. Your Honours, shortly after 8.00 a.m. on 12 August 2001, two days after the mine incident at Ljubotenski Bacila, a police unit led by Johan Tarculovski entered the north-western end of Ljuboten from the direction of Ljubanci, and this is shown in the panorama photograph with the red line. The path the police unit took came from the right of the picture moving to the left. Your Honours, the terror and the cruelty that this police unit inflicted upon the civilians of Ljuboten over the next five or so hours is simply but starkly illustrated by the words of Witness M-017, as he said at page 630 of the transcript: "I don't know how to describe it. I wouldn't have done what they did to us to an animal." The senseless brutality and the unlawfulness of this tactic was apparent right from the start with the murder of Rami Jusufi. Two eye-witnesses, Elmaz and Zenep Jusufi, have given evidence that at approximately 8.20 a.m., members of Tarculovski's police unit opened the gates and entered their yard, and this location is shown by the point marked with a red "1" on the panorama. Both of these witnesses testified that their son, Rami Jusufi, a 33-year-old ethnic Albanian, was asleep in his bed when the police arrived. They both gave evidence that he awoke and he ran to close the door, and they both gave evidence that when we reached the door he was shot by at least one policeman in their yard. I would ask for Exhibit P4 to now be called up. Your Honours, at the time that Rami Jusufi was shot, he was unarmed; and as we can see from this photograph, he was wearing a light agree T-shirt and blue jeans. Crucially, Peter Bouckaert of Human Rights Watch inspected the scene on 23rd of August, and what he found corroborated the Jusufis version of the events. He found that the gate to the yard had been blown open with explosives, he found bullet casings lying in the yard, and he found bullet holes in the front door. This can be found in Exhibit P352, the Human Rights Watch report, at the page with ERN U000-0104. Bouckaert also found a pool of blood on the carpet just inside the front, and this is the same location where the Jusufis say their son, Rami, was standing when he was shot. Bouckaert found no indications that there had been any firing from the inside the house, and I refer to his 92 ter statement, Exhibit P322, at paragraphs 54 to 55. Now, counsel for the accused have sought to discredit the evidence of Zenep and Elmaz Jusufi. They have pointed to apparent inconsistencies in their testimony. Counsel for the accused Boskoski has gone even further, making the novel argument that the consistencies in their evidence renders their evidence unreliable, as it's apparently an indication that they must have discussed their testimony together, while at the same time saying that any inconsistencies must be proof that they're not telling the truth. This is at paragraph 291 of the Boskoski final brief. Your Honours, the fact is that on all material points, Zenep and Elmaz Jusufi gave consistent and truthful evidence, and that evidence proves that Rami Jusufi was an unarmed civilian taking no part in the hostilities. It proves that he was shot and he was killed by members of Tarculovski's police unit as he stood in the doorway of his home. Your Honours, the Prosecution has satisfied its burden of proofing the murder of Rami Jusufi as charged in the indictment. After the murder of Rami Jusufi, the police unit then moved on to the upper eastern part of Ljuboten arriving at the houses of Adem Ametovski and Zija Ademi. I would ask that the panoramic photograph be brought back up. And, Your Honours, the location I'm referring to now is shown with the red number "2" on the panoramic photograph. At these two homes, a number of villagers, all unarmed and all ethnic Albanian, had taken cover in the basement of these two houses. They had taken cover from the police ground attack and from the shelling from the army positions, and I refer to paragraph 95 of the Prosecution's final brief. The police ordered these men out of the basements. They made them lie down near the main gait where they beat them with boots, fists, and rifle-butts. This is paragraph 96 of the Prosecution's final brief. The police tortured some of the men with burning pieces of wood and they even carved a cross into the back of one man, Ismail Ramadani, as he lay on the ground. That is in paragraph 98 of our final brief. And, Your Honours, I would ask that we move briefly into private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, over the course of this trial, has also heard evidence of the murder at this particular location of two more ethnic Albanians, Sulejman Bajrami and Muharem Ramadani. In the case of Sulejman Bajrami, during the beatings and after a policemen kicked him in the head as he lay on the ground, he stood up, groaning in pain, and started to move away. He was allowed to walk for approximately ten metres before at least one policemen shot and killed him. The remaining detainees were then made to match towards Ljubanci. As they moved off, two elderly men, Muharem Ramadani and Aziz Bajrami, were left behind at the gate to the Ametovski house. However, the evidence indicates that at least one police officer shot at these two unarmed elderly men killing Muharem Ramadani. That could be found in paragraph 100 of the final brief. Again, the Defence have sought to discredit this evidence. With regards to the murder of Sulejman Bajrami, counsel for Tarculovski have suggested that there is conflicting evidence about how he died. They suggest that the possibility could not be excluded that he was killed by cross-fire or by so-called friendly fire; although, they do acknowledge that the police units that they accept was on the ground in Ljuboten may also have killed him. I refer to paragraph 260 of the Tarculovski final brief. With respect, Your Honours, there is no conflicting evidence here. The only reliable evidence before the Court is that the police unit killed Sulejman Bajrami; anything else is pure conjecture. Counsel for both accused also contend that Bajrami was attempting to escape and was, therefore, a legitimate target for the police. I refer to paragraph 264 of the Tarculovski brief and paragraphs 299 to 302 of the Boskoski brief. This argument is flawed on a number of levels. First, the evidence shows that Sulejman Bajrami was an unarmed civilian. He was not taking an active part in hostilities; therefore, he was not a prisoner of war. He was an unlawfully detained civilian. Second, he got up and he moved away out only after he'd beaten and kicked in the head while lying on the ground. He was not attempting to escape custody. He was trying to end the vicious beating that the police were giving him. Furthermore, the eye-witness testimony is clear that the police allowed Bajrami to move away. They made no effort to stop this dazed, unarmed man from leaving. There were no cries for him to stop; instead, they allowed him to move away, watching him go, before simply shooting him. I refer to paragraph 97 of the Prosecution's final brief. Your Honours, if we could move briefly into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The scenario which I have just described is corroborated by Henry Bolton, who testified that his examination of Bajrami's body lead him to the conclusion that Bajrami was shot from close range while his body was on or close to the ground. This is at page 1809 of the transcript. The evidence shows that what took place was the execution of a wounded man lying on the ground. Even if he had been taking active part in hostilities, which the Prosecution does not concede, and even if he been trying to escape, what took place was simply murder. The evidence regarding the killing of Muharem Ramadani is equally unequivocal. The only evidence before this Court is that he was killed by the police at the gate to the Ametovski house. Counsel for Boskoski has suggested that cannot be ruled out that Ramadani was killed by fire from the army positions or by NLA position, and my learned colleague cite from Henry Bolton testimony to indicate that the bullet that shot Ramadani could have come from as far as 150 metres away. This assertion is in paragraph 304 of Boskoski's final brief. With respect, Your Honours, this passage that they cite comes from a discussion of Sulejman Bajrami, not Muharem Ramadani, and it is simply describes the line of site around Bajrami that Bolton used as the starting point for his analysis of the distance from which Bajrami was shot. I refer to the transcript page 1809. In fact, Bolton's opinion was that Muharem Ramadani, like Sulejman Bajrami, had been shot from close range. I refer to Exhibit 1D24, with the page with the ERN N001-5357. Then, in their final briefs, counsel for both accused also seek to justify the murders of Sulejman Bajrami and Muharem Ramadani and the cruel treatment of the 11 other men taken from the basement by alleging that all these men are in some way actively engaged in hostilities. In support of this theory, our learned colleagues refer to a gun and ammunition found in the basement of the Ametovski house. They refer to the evidence of Henry Bolton on this point at pages 1701 and 1702. They insist that this evidence proves that these men were shooting at the Macedonian security forces. In fact, Henry Bolton's evidence was that this gun that was found was a shotgun of the type used for hunting birds. It was not a high-velocity rifle of the type used in combat. This is it at page 1702 of the transcript. He is also gave evidence that this shotgun was just one of several items, and a number of items that appear to have been in the basement for sometime, and that they were not signs that it had been hidden or rapidly discarded or that had been fired any time recently. I refer to his 92 ter statement at paragraph -- sorry, Exhibit P236.1, paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the Prosecution to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Clearly, Your Honours, there is nothing suspicious or sinister in the presence of this bird gun in the basement of the Ametovski house. Counsel for Tarculovski also referred to evidence apparently indicating that all the men in the Ametovski house were combatants, who had been firing towards the police with weapons that they later hid in a fridge freezer in the basement. This is found in paragraph 265 of the Tarculovski brief. This evidence, however, is nothing more than an unsubstantiated, third-hand, hearsay rumour. This information comes from an unnamed source, and it was provided to the MOI some seven months after the events in Ljuboten. This is contained in Exhibit 1D273. There is nothing else in evidence to support this rumour. On the contrary, Bolton gave evidence that during his on-site inspection on 14 August, as he moved along the road towards the Jashari house, and that is the same road that the Ametovski house is located, although he found evidence indicating that the police had been firing as they moved from west to east, he found no evidence of any fire coming from the other direction towards the police unit. I refer to Exhibit P236.1, paragraph 13. Furthermore, Your Honours, it defies belief that the police would detain these unarmed men, supposedly with the genuine belief that they were combatants who had been firing at them, and then not even search the basement for the supposed collection of weapons. The police didn't find any such weapons because there were none to be found, and the police didn't search for any weapons because they did not believe that these men were combatants. This was confirmed when Bolton went into the basement himself on 14 August and found nothing apart from the previously mentioned bird gun. As the police marched the ten remaining detainees from the Ametovski house toward Ljubanci, the beatings continued. These men arrived at a police check-point at a residence known as Brace's house at the Ljuboten-Ljubanci border. This can be seen on the panoramic photograph. It is a blue circle with a yellow flag coming up on the right-hand side of the picture. M-037 testified that Johan Tarculovski was also present at Brace's house on the afternoon of 12 August, and I refer to transcript pages 873 to 875. And, Your Honours, could we briefly move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: At Brace's house, the police continued to beat the detainees until they were eventually loaded on a truck and taken to Mirkovci police station. That's at page 897 to 899 of the transcript. The police did not, as suggested by counsel for Tarculovski at paragraph 309 of the brief, "transport the men outside of the danger." They were simply transported from one location where they were being beaten, that is Brace's house, to another location where they were being beaten, that is Mirkovci police station, and they were beaten while they were being transported there. I refer to paragraph 121 of the Prosecution's final brief. At Mirkovci police station, although he was unable to even speak at this time, the police continued to beat Atulla Qaili. Eventually, he was transported to Skopje City Hospital where he died from his injuries on 13 August. In their final briefs, the Defence have attempted to portray Atulla Qaili, not as an unarmed civilian, but as a heavily armed combatant. This assertion cannot be supported by any reasonable interpretation of the evidence. The Trial Chamber has heard from Drs. Stein, Eichner, and Jakovski, who all attested to the inherent unreliability of the paraffin glove test as a means of determining whether an individual has fired a weapon. Yet still, counsel for Tarculovski contend that there is a high probability that Atulla Qaili was an NLA member, and this assertion is based solely on the paraffin glove test that was apparently performed on him at his autopsy. This is at paragraph 272 of the Tarculovski final brief. The evidentiary value of the paraffin glove test is clear; it is minimal at best. Counsel for Boskoski then assert there is evidence that, when detained, Atulla Qaili was found in possession of hand-grenades. I refer to paragraph 311 of the Boskoski final brief. However, despite what one would expect to find if this were true, such as Official Notes or criminal reports from the MOI, there are no such documents and evidence containing any such allegations. In fact, this evidence about a hand-grenade is nothing more than a rumour that was put to OTP investigator Thomas Kuehnel during cross-examination. It is nothing more than this, and this can be found at page 8046 of the transcript. Finally, our learned colleagues have suggested that a bullet that might have come from Atulla Qaili's clothing was recovered from close to his body when exhumed. This is at paragraph 311 of the Boskoski final brief. In fact, the bullet was found on top the ground in the general area of Atulla Qaili's grave the day before the exhumation took place, several months after his death. I refer to transcript pages 5442 to 5445. This, Your Honours, was after he had been detained in the village, held at Mirkovci police station, taken to Skopje City Hospital for treatment, and had an autopsy performed on him. Yet, somehow it suggested that this bullet remained on his person and escaped the attention of all these people at these various location. There is clearly no connection between Atulla Qaili and this bullet. The claim that Atulla Qaili was in possession, and to quote my learned colleagues, "an arsenal of weaponry at the time of his detention" is completely unsupported by the facts. On the other hand, the facts do show that he was beaten by police while he was detained in Ljuboten at Brace's house and at Mirkovci police station, and that he died as a result of these beatings. Following the murders of Rami Jusufi, Sulejman Bajrami, and Muharem Ramadani, and while the ten detainees from the Ametovski house were taken to Brace's house, the police unit continued to move further east through the village to the house of Kadri Jashari. This is marked by the red number "3" on the panorama. As set out in detail in the Prosecution's final brief, five unarmed civilians taking cover at the Jashari house were driven out and shot at by the police unit who killed three of the men, Xhelal Bajrami, Bajram Jashari, and Kadri Jashari. This is in paragraphs 104 to 119 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask counsel to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: -- of the Prosecution's final brief. In the Defence final briefs, our learned colleagues submit that these victims were, in fact, actively participating in the hostilities. The Prosecution does not accept this position but will rest on the submissions made in the Prosecution's final brief on this point. Further ore, contrary to the forensic and ballistic evidence to eye-witness testimony, and to the conclusions drawn during the on-site investigation carried out by Henry Bolton, counsel for Tarculovski contend that these three men were, in all likelihood, shot by army snipers. The evidence does not support this assertion; and, again, the Prosecution will rely on the points made in its final brief. Now, the evidence that has been put before the Trial Chamber has also shown that as the police units led by Johan Tarculovski moved through the village on 12 August, they left a trail of destruction in their wake. This unit damaged or completely destroyed at least 14 homes through the use of hand-grenades, small arms, and accelerants. The Defence also suggests that police directed their fire -- sorry, Your Honours, if I can just go back a moment. Counsel for Boskoski contend that the damage done to the properties was limited in scope both in terms of the number of properties concerned and the nature of the damage which they characterise as in most cases minimum. This is in paragraph 316 of the Boskoski final brief. With regard to the number of homes damaged, Your Honours, we have established 14 homes in the small close-knit village. In this context, the Prosecution has certainly met its burden of proving that a considerable number of objects were destroyed or damaged. This is test applied by the Strugar Trial Chamber at paragraph 294. With regard to the Defence' position that the damage to the houses was minimal, I would simply refer to the Trial Chamber to the photographs taken by Peter Bouckaert and the International Management Group; for example, I would refer to Exhibits P337, P412.07, P347, and P350. These and other photographs make perfectly clear the damage and destruction that the police units inflicted on these homes is anything but minimal. These homes were left unhabitable. The Defence also suggests that the police directed their fire only at those houses from which they came under fire. Counsel for the accused Tarculovski, in particular, relies upon the evidence of Nikolce Grozdanovski to establish locations from where this hostility fire was allegedly coming, and the Prosecution does not concede that there was shooting from these locations. However, for the sake of argument for this closing submission, the Prosecution has taken a panoramic photograph that was annotated by Grozdanovski, which is Exhibit 1D281, and transposed the alleged locations of hostility fire onto the panoramic being used for this presentation. You will see four locations, four positions on the map labelled A to D. Your Honours, while Grozdanovski clearly located four, and only four, specific buildings from which he claimed fire was coming, Tarculovski's unit damaged or destroyed a minimum of 14 homes, as set out in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask the counsel do slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators. As set out in paragraph 154 of the Prosecution's final brief, Bouckaert's inspection of the village corroborates the allegations that these homes were destroyed by the police and not by army shelling, with clear signs that accelerants were used to set houses alight from the inside. He also found no signs of outgoing fire from these houses. So this destruction of 14 homes, when only four locations had been identified, clearly had nothing to do with the legitimately responding to hostility fire. It's clear from the evidence that the wanton destruction was, indeed, wanton. It was indiscriminate, and it was unrelated to any legitimate military targets. The Trial Chamber has also heard evidence over the past year that shows without any doubt that numerous male ethnic Albanian residents from Ljuboten were detained and were subjected to cruel treatment at a number of locations outside Ljuboten. Residents were detained and beaten repeatedly by police and, with their encouragements, villagers at Buzalak check-point. Detainees from Buzalak check-point were then taken in separate groups to Cair, Kisela Voda, Bit Pazar, and Karpos police stations where the beatings continue. Many were even subjected to cruel treatment at the court and at Skopje City Hospital. This was done by the police and, with their encouragement or approval, civilians. These facts are set out in detail of the Prosecution's final brief at paragraphs 173 to 149. Before concluding this part of the Prosecution's closing statement, I would like to briefly address the general point regarding the reliability of the crime-base witnesses. On all material facts, Your Honours, the evidence of the crime-base witnesses has remained consistent and unchanged. The crime-base witnesses have remained steadfast in their identification of the perpetrators of these crimes. They were either uniformed police officers or, in some of the cases of cruel treatment, civilians acting with the permission and encouragement of the police. The crime-base witnesses have also consistently and steadfastly maintained that when beaten and physically abused by the police, they were unarmed and they were in custody and they had not taken any part in hostility. But in what counsel of Boskoski refers to as the village story, the Defence alleged that the villagers had discussed their evidence and have changed their evidence during the course of these proceedings. In particular, it's alleged that they have changed their evidence regarding the collateral issuing of whether or not any villagers were members of the NLA. With respect, Your Honours, the material issue here is not whether anyone from Ljuboten may have joined the NLA in 2001, the issue is whether there were any NLA fighters in the village on 12 August 2001. The position of the crime-base witnesses has remained the same from the start. There were none. This is confirmed by Nazim Bushi, commander of the 114th Brigade of the NLA, at pages 5634 to 5639 of the transcript; it is also corroborated by Peter Bouckaert, page 3162 of the transcript; and Witness M-083, at pages 1481 to 1482 of the transcript; and Franz-Josef Hutsch, at transcript pages 2710 to 2711. It is to be expected that some details of some of the witnesses recollection of events would change over time, but those changes that the Defence highlights are not material to this case. Your Honours, through the evidence presented to the Court, the Prosecution submits that we have proven beyond a reasonable doubt the crimes of murder, wanton destruction, and cruel treatment, as alleged in the indictment. At this point, I will happy to answer any questions or else I will turn over to my colleague, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will now present submissions on Mr. Tarculovski's responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute. There is an absolute prohibition on the targeting of civilians in customary international law. Article 50 of Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, whose provisions may largely be viewed as reflecting customary law, further provides that in case of doubt, whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian. The police forces who attacked Ljuboten on 12th August, under Mr. Tarculovski' leadership, violated this principle. They committed crimes against civilians. One of the clearest examples of such conduct was demonstrated by what happened at the Ametovski house that day in Ljuboten. At this house, the police forced the ethnic Albanian men to come out of the basement and one of them shouted to the detainees: Expletive, "you thought Arkan is dead." The detainees were compelled to sing Macedonian national songs and to glorify Arkan. The police carved a cross into the back of one of the ethnic Albanian villagers. What could be a more graphic manifestation of a criminal purpose, carving an Orthodox symbol into the back of an ethnic Albanian? As Mr. Dobbyn has just elaborated, as soon as the villagers came out of the basement, the police beat them brutally and killed two men in the group after they had been detained. The detained villagers were also persons not taking an active part in the hostilities and, therefore, protected under Article 3 of the Statute. Next door, women and children were hiding in another basement with some other men from the village, further evidence that those detained were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: May we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: But, as we have heard, the crimes at the Ametovski house were not the only crimes committed in Ljuboten that day. There was a pattern of crimes that occurred throughout the village, including murders, wanton destruction, and further acts of cruelty perpetrated against the ethnic Albanian villagers by the police forces who attacked the village. The question is: How could this happen? It happened because the police perpetrators of these crimes wanted them to happen. They intended to commit crimes. The evidence shows that the summer of 2001 was a violent time in Macedonia. Indeed, a Defence witness, Petre Stojanovski, assistant to the head of SVR Skopje in 2001, described as "the practice "acts of violence against civilian property and suspected ethnic Albanian terrorists." In other words, such violence was normal. It was particularly foreseeable after casualties suffered by the Macedonian security forces. The same witness, Petre Stojanovski, agreed that the police, by August 2001, would want to take great care after incidents where members of the security forces were killed, in order to try to avoid danger to civilians in such a volatile environment. I refer to the transcript at 9273 to 9274. Just days before the events in Ljuboten on the 8 August, the NLA killed ten soldiers from Prilep at Karpalak, and violence against ethnic Albanian properties followed. Exhibit P610, for example, which is video footage broadcast on Macedonian television at the time, shows the burning mosque in Prilep. Another Defence witness, Blagoja Markovski, described the reactions after the Karpalak incident as a mass scale psychological situation this. This at transcript page 10.882. Another incident occurred only two days later on the 10th of August, at Ljubotenski Bacila, about five kilometres away from Ljuboten. Eight Macedonian soldiers were killed and two of them were from Ljubanci, where the accused, Mr. Tarculovski, is from. Mr. Tarculovski led his police forces into Ljuboten on the 12 August in this incendiary climate. Furthermore, the police forces he led included criminals. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. This evidence is further corroborated by Exhibit P592. The criminal records included serious bodily injury or serious disturbance to another's health, and I refer to Exhibit P590. Defence witness Popovski confirmed that several persons listed in Exhibit P592 as having criminal records were the same persons who received remuneration from the Ministry of Interior in August and September 2001. Mr. Tarculovski's knowledge that persons in his group included criminals can be inferred from the evidence in P379, his own statement, where he said that he had been in Ljuboten with a large group of men, and that he had known all of them. I refer to the ERN N000-8918 to 8919. Mr. Tarculovski's knowledge can also be inferred from the fact that other persons knew that there were criminals in the group. This evidence considered together gives rise to the only reasonable inference; namely, that Mr. Tarculovski was aware of the criminal pasts of persons who went into Ljuboten with him. One of the modes of responsibility alleged in the case against Mr. Tarculovski is a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution must prove that plurality of persons acted together to implement a common purpose. It should be noted that the common purpose need not have been previously arranged or formulated. It may materialise extemporaneously and be inferred from the facts. I refer to the Stakic appeal judgement at paragraph 64. The participation of the accused in the common purpose is required, although he need not physically commit a specific crime. In addition, a participant in a JCE is not required to be physically present when and where a crime is being committed. In the first form of JCE, all participants must intend to effect the common purpose and to commit the crimes. At paragraph 328 of the Tarculovski final brief, the Defence appears to suggest that an agreement between the parties is required under this mode of responsibility. However, this is not the case, as stated in the Krajisnik trial judgement at paragraph 883. The other modes of responsibility alleged against Mr. Tarculovski, under Article 7(1), are ordering, planning, instigating, and aiding and abetting. I will not dwell here on the legal definitions of these modes of responsibility, which are also set out fully in the Prosecution's final brief. How do we know that there was a common criminal purpose with regard to the crimes committed in Ljuboten? Well, we've already heard the statements of the police forces at the Ametovski house that day, which constitutes strong evidence of the criminal purpose. We also know that these events took place at a time when violence against ethnic Albanians constituted the practice, particularly after casualties suffered by the Macedonian security forces. May we go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also an attempt to show that the villagers from the Ametovski house were terrorists; in other words, to frame them as terrorists. The police allegedly found three weapons and ammunition near the Jashari house, but the villagers detained at another location, the Ametovski house, were forced to sign a seizure certificate pertaining to these very weapons. This was a blatant attempt to mask what truly happened that day. There also a number of documents which reflect further attempts to cover up what happened in Ljuboten that day, referred to from page 60 of the Prosecution's final brief. Exhibit P253, for example, a log which recorded Official Notes about events with respect to operational sector Cair doesn't have an entry pertaining to the 12th of August. The report of the first commission, Exhibit P378, is remarkably silent about the death of Atulla Qaili and the grave injuries sustained by Ljuboten villagers in Ljuboten and at the other cruel treatment sites mentioned in the indictment. Where are the reports of cruel treatment regarding all the locations mentioned in the indictment? The Defence makes the claim that a legitimate military purpose existed for the attack in Ljuboten and that the Macedonian security forces believed that the NLA was present in the village. First of all, the NLA was not in Ljuboten, and I refer to the evidence of Bouckaert at T3162; M-083, T1482 to 1482; Witness Grozdanovski at T10.513; Witness Hutsch at T2710 to 11; Witness Bushi at T5634 to 5638. Further, even if the Macedonian security forces had a belief that there were NLA in the village, that does not exclude the concurrent existence of the common criminal purpose. In other words, with regard to criminal purpose, it does not matter. But, of course, the Defence argument begs the question: If the police were indeed going after the NLA and directed its attack against selected targets, as the Defence claims, then why beat and kill the villagers whom they had detained? Another submission by the Defence is that the NLA mingled with civilians in the village and that the NLA are the real culprits for what happened to the village. This is at paragraph 235 of the Tarculovski final brief. First of all, whatever actions are alleged against the NLA, are these relevant to Mr. Tarculovski's responsibility? The answer is no. What is at issue in this case is the crimes in the indictment and the accused's responsibility for these crimes. Second, even if one were to consider that the NLA mingled with civilians, a point which the Prosecution does not concede, then police perpetrators, on the 12th of August, should certainly have been in doubt as to whether the persons they attacked were civilians. As stated earlier, customary law states that when in doubt as to a person's civilian status, such a person must be presumed to be a civilian. The Defence for Mr. Tarculovski has also submitted in its brief on several occasions that the role of Mr. Tarculovski in these events was that of a mere monitor. He was there to monitor these events. Well, the evidence which we have set out in our brief, both testimony and documentary evidence, overwhelmingly shows that his role went far beyond that May we now go into private session again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. The next day Mr. Tarculovski met with Despodov again, and in the face of Despodov's persistent refusal to proceed in the absence of an order he swore at Despodov, saying, "With our without you, the action will take place." And I refer to Despodov at T2567. Exhibit P303 similarly records Mr. Tarculovski saying after 2200 hours on the 11th of August, that on the following day, at 4.30 a.m., he would start the action. Again, these words and actions are not those of someone who was merely monitoring the situation. Mr. Tarculovski's participation is reflected in his own statements to the second commission, and I refer to Exhibit P379. In the 3rd March 2003 Official Note, Mr. Tarculovski wrote: "Since I was a local, I knew the terrain, and I headed towards Ljuboten with the other men." In the 25th November 2003 information it is stated: "Mr. Tarculovski replied that he was in Ljuboten with many people, more than 100 persons, and he knew all of them." Again, in the 12th November 2003 minutes, the same information is repeated. I'll say a few words about the reliability of these documents that I've just referred to; that is to say, the documents that are part of Exhibit P379. The Defence submits that no weight should be placed on the evidence contained in this document and that all the statements given by Mr. Tarculovski are unreliable. And that is at paragraph 18 of the Tarculovski brief. The Prosecution disagrees, and I must again go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: After the operation had concluded, Witness Hutsch saw Mr. Tarculovski, and he seemed to be in charge. Witness Kuehnel was familiar with the response to a RFA from the Ministry of Defence, according to which the land operation over the village of Ljuboten was under the leadership of Johan Tarculovski on the 12th of August, 2001. Transcript page 7889 to 7892. The evidence of Mr. Tarculovski's participation proves that he is responsible for all modes of responsibility set out in Article 7(1) of the Statute; namely, as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, and for planning, ordering, instigating, and aiding and abetting the crimes. The evidence pertinent to each mode of responsible under Article 7(1) has been set out in detail in Section 3 of the Prosecution's final brief, so I will only briefly highlight a few points with regard to each mode of responsible at this stage. Regarding the joint criminal enterprise, evidence of the criminal purpose and Mr. Tarculovski's participation therein has already been discussed. His intent to further the common purpose is demonstrated by his own statements, his leadership of the operation, the persons he used to carry out the operation, his continuous participation in the attack, and his presence at key locations during the operation, including locations where the crimes occurred. As to ordering, the evidence proves that Mr. Tarculovski was in a position of authority over the physical perpetrators of crimes committed in Ljuboten and that he led the police unit. To cite some examples, on the evening of 11th August he led his unit on a reconnaissance of Ljuboten. A very brief private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: As to planning, the evidence demonstrates that Mr. Tarculovski organised and led the Ljuboten operation; and to cite a few examples, he met with key personnel prior to the operation and requested support for his operation. He procured equipment for his men such as bullet proof vests and radios. As to instigating, the evidence proves that Mr. Tarculovski through his actions and words promoted and substantially contributed to the commission of crimes in Ljuboten. With regard to aiding and abetting, Mr. Tarculovski organised and led the operation and was present at key locations including where crimes occurred. His presence, words, and actions at these locations constituted encouragement of the police forces to commit crimes. He must have been aware of the legitimi sing effect of his words and presence on the actions of the physical perpetrators. Mr. Tarculovski acted with direct intent or was aware of the substantial likelihood that crimes would be committed during the Ljuboten operation. He must have been aware of the volatile climate in Macedonia at the time, the danger to ethnic Albanians, especially after the deaths of Macedonian security force-personnel, and the use of criminals for the operation. The Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber to find Mr. Tarculovski guilty under Article 7(1) of the Statute, pursuant to the charges against him, set out in Counts 1 to 3 of the indictment. That brings me to the end of my submissions, Your Honour, and Mr. Saxon will be making the next set of submissions. I don't know if this is a time for a break or I just hand it over to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, before you continue, the Chamber has been uncertain as to the basis upon which the references to certain evidence was made only in a private session. utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Your Honours, I'm going to be speaking about the responsibility of Mr. Boskoski pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute; Mr. Boskoski's responsibility as a superior. Certainly, I would be happy to respond to any questions that you might have, either during my submissions or after I finish. The evidence proves that Mr. Boskoski's de jure and de facto control over Johan Tarculovski and the police officers who perpetrated crimes in Ljuboten and that cruel treatment in locations outside of Ljuboten and in Skopje, and Boskoski's effective control over police officers whose acts and omissions aided and abetted prison guards, hospital personnel, and civilians to commit the crimes charged in the indictment. The evidence also proves that Mr. Boskoski knew and had reason to know that his subordinates perpetrated and aided and abetted the crimes alleged in the indictment. And, Your Honours for purposes of my submissions when I use the term "indictment," I'm referring to the Second Amended Indictment. Finally, the evidence proves that Mr. Boskoski failed to take all necessary and reasonable measures to punish his subordinates who were responsible for these crimes. I'd like to spend a few minutes discussing Mr. Boskoski's effective control over the perpetrators of the crimes. Paragraphs 274 to 276 of the Prosecution's final brief describe Mr. Boskoski's de facto control over Macedonian police forces, including reserve police officers in 2001. I won't repeat that discussion today, but I would like to refer you to some additional evidence that illustrates the extent of Mr. Boskoski's control over Ministry of Internal Affairs personnel, including police officers, when he was the minister. Your Honours, at pages 5133 to 5134 of the transcript, police General Zoran Jovanovski described how Mr. Boskoski could order one of his directors to obtain more information about an issue, and how those orders would be passed down the ministry's chain of command. And after meetings of Mr. Boskoski's collegium, his subordinate, such as General Jovanovski, would carry out the instructions of the minister. That's at page 5099 of the transcript. Your Honours, on the 28th of July, 2001, Minister Boskoski instructed his subordinates in the ministry to cut short all annual leave being taken at that time, and to direct all employees on annual leave at that time to return to their work. We see this in Exhibit P00489. The Chamber heard from Miodrag Stojanovski that these instructions reached the PSOLO police station. That is it at page 6812 of the transcript. After the Ohrid Framework Agreement was signed on the 13th of August, the Ministry of Internal Affairs chain of command continued to function. Orders were sent down the chain of command and reports went up. General Jovanovski continued to carry out the orders of his superiors. That's at page 5101 of the transcript. Defence witness Keskovski, a member of the ministry's security sector, described how members of the Macedonian army were placed under his command during a period of 2001. That's at page 10.083 of the transcript. Witness M-084, at page 1450, described how at OVR Cair, in 2001, there was a station commander, a department station commander, and an assistant commander. All of these personnel were subordinate to the Ministry of Interior which was in command. And at page 1452 of the transcript, M-084 gave a vivid description of the place of the minister in that chain of command, and the amount of power that he exercised. He said: "The minister of the interior has the right to issue an order anywhere and any time, and no one could tell him whether that would be at 4.00 a.m. or 4.00 p.m." As M-052 described the power of the minister, at page 8438: "The minister is my superior. I do not, I cannot doubt his word." Your Honours, along with this evidence, authority cited by counsel for Mr. Boskoski in his final brief, at footnote 966, helps us understand the military dynamics that were alive in the Ministry of Internal Affairs during 2001. In the article called, "Command responsibility for war crimes," the author explains on the first page: "That subordinates typical obey is a basic tenet of military life." The evidence in this trial proves beyond a reasonable doubt that this military principle was alive and well in the Ministry of Internal Affairs in 2001. For example, Witness M-056 described how: "There are strict sanctions for not obeying orders." This is at page 2168 of the transcript. Indeed, during 2001, not only was there a chain of command operating within the Ministry of Internal Affairs, there were also diverse chains of command operating at that time within that one ministry. For example, the commander of the Tigers special police units reported to two chains of command, to the minister and to the directors of the bureau for public safety and the counter-intelligence directorate. You'll find that testimony at page 2133. Your Honours, above Minister Boskoski in the chain of command was the prime minister, Ljubco Georgievski. In his expert report, Dr. Blagoja Markovski confirmed that the prime minister commanded the police through the minister of interior. That's at Exhibit 2D101, paragraph 216. For example, at the beginning of the armed conflict, Prime Minister Georgievski instructed the commander of the Tigers special police unit to expand that unit. This is it at pages 2253 to 2256. All of this evidence, Your Honour, is further proof of the effective control that Mr. Boskoski exercised over members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the police. As you know, the element of effective control is important as a manifestation of the superior/subordinate relationship required to prove criminal responsibility under Article 7(3) of our Statute. Your Honour, the evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the members of the unit led by Johan Tarculovski in Ljuboten village were reserve police officers. We know that the men who followed Mr. Tarculovski into Ljuboten were police reservists for several reasons. The members of Mr. Tarculovski's unit were "given weapons and uniforms and put on the list at PSOLO police station and at OVR Cair." That met the standards for becoming a police reservist that you will find described at page 8430 to 8432 of the transcript. As witness M-084 explained, pages 1460 to 1462, with respect to the men who received weapons on the 10th of August: "Data was taken and their criminal record checked. Those who did not have a criminal record were given weapons." In the words of M-084: "The competence after the reserve police officer wears the clothes and takes the weapons, then the competence and responsibility is assumed by the superior officers in the station." As M-052 put it succinctly at page 8433 of the transcript: "If a person wears a uniform, he is employed in the ministry." Second of all, Your Honours, the men were deployed and subordinated to a regular police officer, Mr. Tarculovski, who in turn, was a subordinate of Mr. Boskoski. This requirement is described by Witnesses M-053 and M-084, pages 1990 and 1460 respectively. It is also corroborated by Miodrag Stojanovski who testified that: "One such volunteers were redeployed they were subordinated to the commanders of the units where they were assigned," at pages 6838 to 6839. Third, Your Honours, Mr. Tarculovski, the leader of the group of men who entered Ljuboten on the 12th of August, said that they were reservists. You can find that at his Official Note from May 2003. It is part of Exhibit P00379, bearing ERN N000-8922. M-052 described how the people who went into Ljuboten on the 12th of August were "police," so did Defence witness Army Captain Grozdanovski at page 10.511 of the transcript. Other Prosecution and Defence witnesses who served in the Macedonian army at that time confirmed that the army of the Republic of Macedonia did not enter Ljuboten on the 12th of August. We heard that from Witness 2D008, at page 10576; from Mr. Despodov, at page 2597; from witness M-051, at pages 4136 to 4137; and from Mr. Jurisic, at page 3319. And, finally, Your Honour, even the Tarculovski Defence acknowledges that the unit that entered Ljuboten on the 12th of August were police officers. If you look at the final brief of the Tarculovski Defence, ten times from paragraphs 205 to 210, five times in paragraph 265 alone, and, additionally, in paragraphs 276, 277, 278, and 308 in the brief, we are told that there were police in the village. Your Honours, as explained at paragraphs 303 to 307 of the Prosecution's brief, by the summer of 2001, the Ministry of Internal Affairs did not depend on the fulfilment of formal administrative so-called requirements for the mobilisation of police reservists. Instead, ministry officials focussed on de facto indicator, such as the issuance of weapons and uniforms and the deployment with a regular police officer; nor should any de jure requirements, if they existed, be determinative of Mr. Boskoski's effective control over these police officers. In the Blaskic trial judgement at paragraph 302, the Trial Chamber held that superiors need not have any legal authority to prevent or punish acts of subordinates. The determining factor is a superior's material ability to do so. In this case, the evidence demonstrates Mr. Boskoski's de facto and de jure powers over all police reservists, whether or not they had fulfilled all potential conditions described in laws and by-laws. The fact that police reservists stood at attention when Mr. Boskoski entered the courtyard of Brace's house on the 12th of August, 2001 is a much more germane indication of a superior/subordinate relationship than compliance with administrative criteria. I'm referring, Your Honours, to the testimony of Mr. Jakovoski at page 3938 and also to testimony at page 8281. Your Honours, there is another reason why it would be incorrect to give too much importance to the supposed de jure requirements for police reservists. The evidence demonstrates that during the summer of 2001, police command positions, even entire police units, existed de facto before they existed de jure. For example, at pages 8610 to 8611, the Chamber heard how the Kuceviste reserve police station and the work of Marjan Taskovski, as the commander of that police station, began before the Ministry of Internal Affairs issued a decision establishing that reserve police station on 15 August 2001. Mr. Taskovski complained several times about the fact that he was working as the commander of this reserve police station, but he was not yet receiving the appropriate salary because no decision had been issued formally appointing him to that position. And in that same testimony, M-052 explained that these kinds of situations arose frequently during that crisis period. Indeed, Your Honours, the testimony of Witness M-056, at pages 2235 to 2237, illustrates a similar situation involving positions in the posebna unit, which existed long before rules were issued establishing those positions. Furthermore, Your Honour, the genesis of the Ministry of Internal Affairs Lions unit provides another example where de facto situations existed on the ground long before they were formalised. I would refer you to Exhibit P00074, a decision issued by Mr. Boskoski on the 6th of August to establish a rapid intervention battalion, composed of regular members of the special units of the police, the posebna unit, regular police, and members of the police reserve. This units, Your Honours, became known as the Lions. Jovanovski testified that a majority of the members of this unit came from the posebna unit. That's at page 4909 of the transcript. During his cross-examination, Jovanovski agreed that the establishment of the Lions unit was not complete until mid-November 2001, when the members received employment contracts with the Ministry of Internal Affairs. This is at pages 4907 to 4911. However, in his memoire of those years, Mr. Boskoski acknowledged that the Lions unit operated as a "special reserve unit of the Ministry of Internal Affairs" well before November. By late August 2001, Mr. Boskoski acknowledged to the media that: "The newly formed forces called the Lions are not a paramilitary group of armed civilians, as Western diplomates claim," but, rather, a special Ministry of Internal Affairs reserve unit. This special reserve unit, Mr. Boskoski explained to the Reuters news service, would conduct "search and destroy operations up and down the entire length of western Macedonia." Persons found in possession of weapons would "be punished more harshly than usual." You can find this information, Your Honour, in Exhibit P00402, in the English translation bearing N000-9661 to N000-9685, pages 6 to 8. Mr. Boskoski's statements in this regard in his book are supported by the transcript to Exhibit P00439, a video-clip of Mr. Boskoski and the Lions unit in November 2001. Your Honours, also relevant to the genesis of the Lions is Exhibit P00518, an Official Note from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, dated the 22nd of September, 2001, describing the presence of a "battalion for rapid intervention" at the police academy in Idrizovo at that time. That is six weeks before this unit was formally established in November, and discussing concerns that police forces would prevent ethnic Albanian police recruits from entering the police academy. Your Honours, if entire special units could operate in 2001 in a de facto sense before their formal creation in a de jure sense, then surely individuals could be deployed as police reservists and subordinated to the ministry's chain of command before they fulfilled all formal or administrative criteria. In addition, Your Honours, the arguments presented by Mr. Boskoski in his final brief about the existence of prerequisites to becoming a police reservist are also inconsistent with Mr. Boskoski's expert evidence. If you look at paragraph 46 of Exhibit 1D00310, Professor Taseva describes five conditions that must be fulfilled before a person could become a police reservist. One of these requirements was the provision of regular identification documentation. But when we read paragraph 4 of the Boskoski final brief, this requirement of an identification document has disappeared. If the Boskoski Defence is disagreeing with its own expert on this issue, or, if the expert witness was wrong on this matter, then, in the Prosecution's respectful submission, the Chamber should be cautious before it places a great deal of weight or reliance on this argument concerning alleged prerequisites for police reservists in 2001. But for the sake of argument, I would like to consider with you the alleged de jure requirements for mobilisation into the police reserves mentioned by Mr. Boskoski at paragraph 4 of his brief. The first requirement is listing as reservists at the department for defence preparations at the SVR level. Your Honours, the Prosecution concedes that a great deal of evidence was led during this trial, describing the lists of reservists maintained by the Ministry of Defence and by the department of defence preparations within the Ministry of Internal Affairs; for example, at pages 1453 to 1455 of the transcript. However, we know from Mr. Tarculovski's Official Note from May 2003, part of Exhibit 379 as I have said, that the reserve police officers who accompanied him into Ljuboten registered with the reserve as volunteers. The evidence demonstrates that these volunteer police reservists were subjected to a vetting process, including the review of information about them on lists kept by the Ministry of Internal Affairs' department for defence preparations. Your Honour, in 2001 -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. Can we move into private session for one brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The MOI's -- the Ministry of Internal Affairs's department for defence preparations had data provided from the Ministry of Defence on each volunteer which they reviewed at OVR Cair, and then checked to see whether the volunteers had criminal records. You'll find this at page 1455 of the transcript and also from the testimony of M-083 at page 1419. The evidence proves that persons with criminal records were only mobilised into the police reserve upon the orders of ministry superiors. You can find that at pages 8272 to 8274, page 1895, and page 1475.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: (redacted) in this process, this vetting process, with the group of volunteer reservists who came to OVR Cair on 10 and 11 August, some of whom participated in the Ljuboten operation. This is at 1461 to 1462. Prior to that, on the 25th to 26th of July, Miodrag Stojanovski carried out a somewhat different procession with the group of volunteers from Kometa security company, who came to PSOLO police station along with Mr. Tarculovski. This is at pages 6804 to 6806 and page 6830. Upon the orders of Mr. Stojanovski's superiors, volunteers were issued weapons and sent to another ministry facility in order to fill in reserve police officer questionnaires. Thus, procedures were followed to mobilise these volunteers into the Ministry of Internal Affairs. This was not anarchy, Your Honours. On the contrary, this was a controlled procedure subject to the chain of command of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Secondly, the Defence for Mr. Boskoski argue that before a person became a reservist, in 2001, he had to perform some training. Your Honour, the relevant articles in the Law on Internal Affairs, that's Article 46 from Exhibit P00086, pertaining to mobilisation of police reservists do not set out training as a precondition to an individual becoming a reserve police officer. Article 46 of this Law, says that the ministry can up reservists for training, for exercises, or with respect to the circumstances described in Article 45 of the law. Article 45 describes how police reservists can be mobilised during war, emergencies, or when the public peace and order is disrupted on a large-scale. The law does not say that a prospective reserve police officer must undergo training before that person becomes a reservist. Similarly, Your Honours, the Book of Rules for summoning and engaging members of the reserve ranks of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Exhibits 1D0054 and 1D00356, contains no prerequisite of training before a person can join the police reserves. Indeed, Article 2 of that exhibit reads: "The members of the reserve ranks of the ministry take part in practices and other forms of professional training organised by the ministry." In other words, first, the individual becomes a member of the reservists ranks; and, then, he may take part in practices and training. Article 3 of the same by-laws makes the same point, and the first paragraph of that article: "The summoning of members of the ministry for practice or other type of professional training, or, for the performing work and tasks as in Article 2, item 2 of this book of rules, is done by the ministry with an individual or group summons." And in the third paragraph of Article 3: "The individual summons for practice or other type of professional training is delivered by the ministry to the members of the reserve ranks of the ministry." Therefore, Your Honours, the laws and by-laws of the Ministry of Internal Affairs prove that a person became a member of the reserve police forces before he or she would be sent for training. The third criteria mentioned in the Boskoski final brief is payment of compensation; but, Your Honours, nothing in the Law on Internal Affairs or the by-laws of the Ministry of Internal Affairs require that a police reservist receive compensation prior to his or her deployment as a police reservist. Article 4 of the Law on Internal Affairs, P86, provides only that members of the reserve forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs "have the right" to compensation for their service in the reserves. In other words, first comes service; then comes compensation. A discussion during the testimony of police General Zoran Jovanovski shines a particular light on this issue. Starting at the bottom of page 4917 of the transcript, my learned colleague asked General Jovanovski: "In order to become a member of the reserve forces of the Republic of Macedonia, is it true that it is necessary, first, for a person to respond to a summons or to volunteer, in case the summons were public. Answer: "Yes." Question: "Then, to -- for weapons and uniform to be issued?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Then, to go through a brief training which, in 2001, took place in Idrizovo, to receive the identification from the reserve forces, and to be put on the payroll in order to receive the remuneration for the reserve forces?" Answer: "Yes. When the members of the reserve forces are involved for more than one month, and that person -- that person's regular job is put on hold and he receives his salary from the Ministry of Interior." General Jovanovski's evidence indicates that a police reservist could be engaged for less than one month and not have his name placed on the Ministry of Internal Affairs's payroll list. Lastly, paragraph 4 of the Boskoski's brief mentioned age requirements; but there has been no evidence in this trial to suggest that any of the men who followed Mr. Tarculovski into Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001 were minors or were elderly. So if this requirement exists, it is not applicable to this case. Turning to a different topic, Your Honours, at pages 341 to 353 of its final brief, the Prosecution described the abundant evidence which proves that Mr. Boskoski knew or had reason to know that his subordinates perpetrated the crimes alleged in the indictment. I do not intend to review this material today; however, I'm certainly prepared to respond to any questions that you might have about this topic. Moving to the third prong of superior responsibility, I would like to discuss Mr. Boskoski's failure to discharge his duty to punish the perpetrators of the crimes charged in the indictment. At paragraphs 353 to 390 of its final brief, the Prosecution discussed evidence that demonstrates that Mr. Boskoski failed to discharge his duty to take all necessary and reasonable measures to punish his subordinates who perpetrated the crimes charged in the indictment, and I would like to make some additional submissions on this topic today. Once the Prosecution has demonstrated that the accused knew or had reason to know that a subordinate was about to commit a crime, or had done so, the law of superior responsibility does not require the Prosecution to prove further elements of the accused's intent. However, in this case, the evidence proves that Mr. Boskoski's intention was to ensure that none of his subordinates were held accountable for the crimes charged in the indictment. A review of this evidence is pertinent to the third prong of superior responsibility. Your Honours, you can often tell if someone understands how wrong their actions are, and in this case, the actions of a person's subordinates, by the lengths that they go -- the lengths to which they go to rationalise them. For example, in Mr. Boskoski's memoire, Exhibit P00402, at page 6 of the ERN translation N000-9794 to N000-9711, Mr. Boskoski writes: "You know very well that Macedonia and the Macedonian people are dissatisfied with the way the international community acts within our country, and also with its positions regarding Macedonia. In particular, it disagrees with the continuing attempts to equate the victim with the aggressor. The political court in The Hague is a brilliant invention which has nothing to do with human rights at all. It is a pure farce. Why? Because it is being used to incriminate the Macedonian security forces for alleged crimes in Ljuboten where the Macedonian security forces actually saved Ljuboten." I would refer you, again, Your Honours, to the language of Exhibit P378, the report of the 2001 commission created by Mr. Boskoski to review the circumstances and analyse the activities of the Ministry of Interior forces in Ljuboten at page 3: "In such situations, the reality cannot be ignored that in these circumstances, there is both the human factor and a natural reaction to survive in conditions where, in fact, his live has been placed there real danger, and it is precisely this factor, which, in the actions and the activities carried out in the village of Ljuboten caused, in a negligible number of individual events within tolerable limits the established equilibrium of attack defence to be destroyed." Similarly, Your Honour, in Exhibit P00531, an opinion that he sent to the Macedonian government in November 2001, Mr. Boskoski proposed that the government of the Macedonia decline to support a resolution from an ethnic Albanian political party, criticising the use of force by members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Mr. Boskoski argued that the numbers of cases of excessive force was insignificant, "especially having in mind the current security situation in the country." But the laws of wars, Your Honours, presume that a nation can adequately perform its military campaigns without committing crimes. This principle is described in the article, "Command responsible for war crimes," published in the 82nd Yale Law Journal at page 1274, and it's referred to in the final brief of Mr. Boskoski at footnote 966. Mr. Boskoski's attempts to rationalise the misconduct of his subordinates, contrary to international humanitarian, illustrate not only his knowledge of their criminal behaviour but Mr. Boskoski's own desire to minimise these events as unimportant. Indeed, the mention of crimes committed against ethnic Albanians was cause for Mr. Boskoski not to redress these problems but to attack the messenger. On two occasions on television in January 2002, Mr. Boskoski called the leader of the Macedonian Helsinki Committee, state enemy number 1 for her reporting of abuses committed against ethnic Albanians. We learn this from Peter Bouckaert at transcript pages 3262 and 3195. Concurrently, Mr. Boskoski made no genuine efforts to investigate and punish the detailed allegations of egregious abuses committed by his subordinates between 12 and 14 August, 2001. Perversely and effectively, Mr. Boskoski attacked the innocent and protected the guilty. Minister Boskoski's message and intentions remained the same during the spring of 2002. In Exhibit P00277, a video of a speech that Mr. Boskoski gave to the Lions on the 7th of May, 2002, Mr. Boskoski said: "I know that the accusations will continue but the Macedonian public is asking itself why. It is it to defend the fatherland, to defend the constitutional order. What is it that we want to condemn? No, the only thing that can be condemned is treason. That which will not be preserved for the future." The evidence admitted during this trial proves that Mr. Boskoski's intent vis-a-vis the Ljuboten matters was not to perform his legal duties. It was to avoid them, and avoid them he did. The gross failures of the so-called investigation carried out by Mr. Boskoski's closest subordinates in the ministry proves the wish of Mr. Boskoski and his closest colleagues not to identify which members of the Ministry of Interior perpetrated the crimes in and around Ljuboten and Skopje. How else can you explain their failure to probe this matter more deeply? If Mr. Boskoski had insisted that this question be investigated with any skill and sincerity, he would have had to confront his own responsibility as a superior for the actions of his subordinates. This evidence illustrating Mr. Boskoski's intentions during 2001 and 2002 underlines and explains Mr. Boskoski's failure to discharge his obligations as a superior concerning the crimes charged in the indictment. Turning more specifically to this failure, Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski failed to even denounce these crimes. By this failure, Mr. Boskoski failed to take even the simplest most basic step within his ability to identify and punish the perpetrators. Your Honours, the Prosecution does not concede that the Ministry of Internal Affairs was constrained in its investigation by the fact that the public prosecutor and investigating judges were alerted to the death of five persons in Ljuboten on the 12th of August. As discussed in the Prosecution's brief at paragraph 381, the Ministry of Internal Affairs only provided information to the judiciary about alleged acts of terrorism committed by ethnic Albanian residents in Ljuboten. The Ministry of Internal Affairs provided no information to the judiciary about crimes committed against ethnic Albanians on the 12th of August and subsequent days. To paraphrase M-052: "Everybody was there, everybody saw." But no member of the Ministry of Internal Affairs alerted the public prosecutor and the investigative judge to these facts, and the ultimate responsibility for this failure lay with Mr. Boskoski. Even assuming, for the sake of argument, that the judiciary took jurisdiction over all the events alleged in the indictment, additional measures for redressing these crimes were within Mr. Boskoski's abilities. For example, if you look at Article 173 of Exhibit P00096, the Book Of Rules for conducting matters of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, that Article provides: "A special report to the competent public prosecutor shall also be submitted as a supplement to the criminal charges in the case when, after criminal charges are brought, new facts, evidence, or traces of a crime are determined." In this matter, had the Ministry of Internal Affairs conducted a serious investigation, it could have provided the facts of the crimes, the identities of the perpetrators, or even the facts that serious allegation existed about the crimes, to the public prosecutor. As minister, Mr. Boskoski had the power to instruct his subordinates to produce such a "special report" and provide it to the public prosecutor. Instead, Mr. Boskoski chose to categorically deny that any serious misconduct occurred or to minimise the significant of that misconduct. The Ministry of Internal Affairs could have submitted a copy of the Human Rights Watch report now in evidence in this case to the investigative judge and the public prosecutor. But a review of the court files from Basic Court I in Skopje, that is Exhibits P46 through P55, reveals that this simple measure did not occur. Given his legal duty to investigate and punish, Mr. Boskoski could not have relied on the results of his own sham investigative commission. Your Honour, the president of Macedonia in 2001, Boris Trajkovski, told representatives of the international community in November of that year that he had no faith in Macedonian government commissions because they produced no results. That's in Exhibit 1D00211. And that statement is significant for two reasons. First, it illustrates that commissions established to redress serious issues, such as the conduct of the Ministry of Internal Affairs forces in Ljuboten, were mere facades; and, secondly, it illustrates implicitly that not even the president, a member of Mr. Boskoski's own political party, had faith in the work of Mr. Boskoski's commission set up to review the conduct of his subordinates in the village of Ljuboten. Your Honours, the cooperation, or lack thereof, of ethnic Albanian victims of the crimes committed between 12 and 14 August with Macedonian authorities does not excuse the failure of Mr. Boskoski to take all necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators. For example, in the judgement rendered in the case of Maritza Urrutia versus Gautemala on the 27th November 2003, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights noted at paragraph 104(d) that: "The obligation to investigate cannot depend on the decision of the victim." Your Honours, the complex security situation existing in Macedonia during 2001 and 2002 did not prevent the Ministry of Interior from performing more thorough investigation into the allegations of the crimes described in the indictment. You heard the testimony of Deputy Public Prosecutor Vilma Ruskovska at pages 1523 to 1524 of the transcript. Ms. Ruskovska described how, in the summer of 2001, she received telephone threats from the NLA and how these threats frightened her. But Ms. Ruskovska continued to carry out her professional responsibilities because, as she explained, "as a prosecutor, you know that our profession is such. We do receive threats, but we need to -- but we need to continue working having this in mind. We either accept our job as it is, or we discontinue working at it." That same simple principle applied to Mr. Boskoski and the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Mr. Boskoski remained in his position, with all of its duties, powers, and responsibilities, throughout the time-period described in the indictment. Furthermore, Your Honours, the fact that the Macedonian government had not yet created a formal witness protection programme provides no excuse for Mr. Boskoski's failure to discharge his obligations in this case. In reality, Minister Boskoski had his own witness protection capability. I'd like to show you a bit of video material, please. This will be Exhibit P00277. It was shot in November 2001. It shows the Lions -- members of the Lions, the Tigers, and the posebna units in an exercise attended by Mr. Boskoski and the prime minister. If we could play that tape, please.

Your Honours, that was Mr. Boskoski's witness protection programme had he chosen to use it, and it existed long before the events in Ljuboten. Given the man power, the weaponry, the armoured personnel carriers, and the facilities available to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, protecting witnesses who were members of that ministry would have been a very feasible task.
