The Hermeline accomplished its task with one exception. There was one clumsy police reservist, Aleksander Janevski, also known as Kunta the younger or Kunta junior, who shot himself in the foot; the only police casualty that day. You find that evidence at pages 8288 to 8289, and pages 8293 and 8295. Fortunately, the Hermeline was available to quickly transport Kunta the younger to Brace's house. That's at pages 864 to 865. Finally, on this point, Your Honours, I would direct your attention to Exhibit P00148, a Ministry of Internal Affairs Official Note, dated 14 August 2001, which indicates that ministry personnel were able to obtain important information from a person born in Ljuboten about the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, such as information pertaining to the identities of the persons killed there. Thus, information was accessible to the Ministry of Internal Affairs even in the tense environment following the events of 12 August. You might also want to review, in this regard, Exhibit 1D189, a similar document dated 15 November 2001. Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski had ample ability to ensure that the police officers who perpetrated the crimes on the 12th -- from the 12th to 14th of August were disciplined. Exhibits P00523 to P00530 provide the proof of Mr. Boskoski's ability to discipline his subordinates when he wished to. Two exhibits, in particular, are worth noting today. If we could move -- or I will try to do this in public session, Your Honour. You may want to refer to Exhibit P00526, which contains the records of the disciplinary proceedings against the former head of the Tigers special police unit. If you scan just the first page of ERN N006-6076 to 6077, you will see how effective the Ministry of Interior's disciplinary system could be, even during the armed conflict. The incident involving that commander at Vaksince occurred on 25 May 2001. The director of the public security sector of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, that was Mr. Mitevski, submitted a proposal to start disciplinary proceedings with the Ministry of Interior's permanent disciplinary committee on the 30th of May, 2001. And on the 9th of July 2001, just 45 days after the incident at Vaksince, and after several procedures, the minister signed a decision confirming the punishment for the individual involved. Clearly, this system could work well, even during the armed conflict, when the leaders of the Ministry of Internal Affairs wanted it to work. In addition, Your Honours, I would respectfully direct the Chamber's attention to Exhibit P00528, disciplinary proceedings brought in early 2002 against a reserve member of the -- excuse me, against a regular member of the police and a police reservist. The head of OVR Cair at that time submitted criminal reports concerning both individuals to the public prosecutor. Your Honours, my colleagues who spoke previously mentioned the pattern of crimes that occurred between the 12th and 14th of August, and I would respectfully ask you during your deliberations to look not just at the pattern of crimes but also at the entire patterns of events subsequent to that -- to those crimes. The evidence demonstrates that the Ministry of Internal Affairs forces were involved in Ljuboten and that they perpetrated the crimes in and around Ljuboten and in and around Skopje. The evidence demonstrates the ministry's failure, Mr. Boskoski's failure, to ensure that easy and obvious investigative tasks were performed. The evidence demonstrates that no reporting was done about these crimes, alleged crimes, to the judiciary. The evidence also demonstrates that this occurred in an environment both before and after the 12th of August, when offer acts of police brutality had been committed against ethnic Albanian civilians. So, Your Honours, in the Prosecution's submission, this evidence demonstrates the failure of Mr. Boskoski to discharge his duty to take all necessary and reasonable measures to investigate these allegations and punish the perpetrators. Unless you have any questions for me, I will turn the microphone over to my colleague, Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm going to address the topic of armed conflict, the chapeau of requirement of Article 3. I am going to structure my presentation in three groups. I will start with the legal standard; then I will move to the most relevant evidence concerning the organisation of the NLA, and I will address my learned colleagues's submissions at this stage; and I will end up my submissions with the key facts concerning the intensity of the armed conflict. Your Honours, I do not intend to repeat the whole Prosecution closing brief; therefore, in case of any omission, I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 391 to 503 where the armed conflict is presented. Now, Your Honours, the legal standard. The test which was originally laid out in the Tadic jurisdiction appeal decision states that an armed conflict exists whenever there is an resort to armed force between states, or protracted violence between governmental authorities and armed groups, or between these groups within a state. Basically, Your Honours, the test focuses on two conditions and two requirements: The intensity of the conflict and the organisation of the parties to the conflict. The criteria of protracted armed conflict has been interpreted in practice as referring more to the intensity of the armed violence than to its duration. I would refer to Your Honours, to Haradinaj trial judgement, paragraph 49. Further, some degree of organisation by the parties will suffice to establish the existence of the armed conflict. Basically, the main purpose of the Tadic test is to distinguish an armed conflict from banditry and organised and short-lived insurrections, as well as terrorist activities which are not subject to international humanitarian law. Your Honours, the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the armed violence through wide scale use of conventional arms between the Macedonian security force, meaning police of the MOI and army, and the NLA between September -- excuse me, from January to September 2001 constituted an armed conflict of a scale that met the intensity prong of the Tadic test. Secondly, Your Honours, the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the NLA had an organised hierarchical structure, as well as a functioning chain of command and logistics, distinctive of an organised armoured group able to engage in an internal armed conflict. The Prosecution, Your Honours, has also proved the existence of a nexus between the crimes and the armed conflict. Both accused where aware of the factual circumstances of the Macedonian conflict, and the existence of this armed conflict play a substantial role in the accused's ability and decision to commit the crimes. Finally, Your Honours, the four Tadic requirements described in the appeal jurisdiction decision, paragraph 94, have also been met. I will refer Your Honours to paragraphs 501 to 503 of the Prosecution closing brief on this regard. Now, Your Honours, I will move to the second part of my submissions, the organisation of the NLA. The NLA had a functioning chain of command and a hierarchical structure with a General Staff in the top, with Ali Ahmeti, the NLA commander; Gzim Ostreni, the Chief of Staff; as well as other members, such Shefit, aka Krabata [phoen], in charge of logistics; or Nazmi Bikari [phoen], dealing -- the spokesperson. And the law of that hierarchical structure, we could find active brigades, and one brigade which was in a state of readiness. Each brigade had its own commanders, zone of operations, headquarters. The Prosecution, Your Honours, has proved these facts through viva voce witness and through documentary evidence coming from different and credible source. We have seen, Your Honours, Exhibit P487, the directive produced by Gzim Ostreni at the beginning of June. We have also presented Exhibit P515, also three maps produced by Gzim Ostreni to be delivered to NATO indicating the areas under the control of the NLA by July -- by the beginning of July 2001. But, Your Honours, we have also presented documents coming from the Macedonian government, such as Exhibit P485, or from NATO such as P493 and P321. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution submission that all these documents are reliable, relevant, and have a probative value to establish the existence of the organisation of the NLA. The Prosecution has presented through Gzim Ostreni, Nazim Bushi, and the expert witness of the Prosecution, Viktor Bezruchenko, the NLA regulations that were intended to organise the diverse needs of the NLA in order to function as an organised army. I will refer Your Honours to the Prosecution's brief, paragraphs 475 to 482. Your Honours, the NLA was able to speak through a unified voice, and they did so through the communiques. The communiques which were issued generally by the General Staff aimed at informing the public about the goals of the NLA, about the actions of the NLA. Even the MOI document, the White Book, P45, acknowledged the existence of the communiques and reproduced the text of these communiques. Your Honours, I won't repeat all the documents which are in evidence, but I would like to highlight three. Communique number 6, Exhibit P520, reproduces the main goals of the NLA which do not include the disintegration of Macedonia. The NLA claims since the very beginning of the armed conflict that they were fighting for equal rights of the Albanian population through political changes such as the amendment of the constitution. But the communique number 6 was not the only document where the cause of the NLA were reproduced. Also there is the Prizren Agreement, reached the 22nd of May between Ali Ahmeti and the two male leaders of the Albanian political parties with representation in the Macedonian parliament, that is Exhibit P560. Also there is the memorandum issued by Ali Ahmeti on the 24th of April, to Kofi Annan, to the leaders of NATO, OSCE, and the European Commission, which was explained by Ostreni in pages 7445, and it's actually acknowledged by the US spokespersons and journalists in the Defence exhibits 1D338, page 4. Your Honours, if we compare the Ohrid Agreement, the text of the Ohrid Agreement, Exhibit P84, with the text of these three documents, we will see an overlap. The demands of the NLA were, indeed, reflected in the Ohrid Agreement despite the fact that NLA was not a signatory party. But, indeed, Ali Ahmeti kept in contact with the parties who were negotiating the Ohrid Agreement. Your Honours, the NLA was also regarded as a valid negotiating party by the international community. Exhibit P514, another communique issued by the Ali Ahmeti, explains how the withdrawal of Aracinovo was agreed upon by Ali Ahmeti and representatives from NATO and European Union. Exhibit P458, another communique issued by Ali Ahmeti on the 14th of August, where he explains how he reach agreement with Peter Feith, the NATO representative, concerning the demobilisation that is found disbandment of the NLA, that what later became Operation Essential Harvest. Therefore, Your Honours, Tarculovski's argument in paragraph 58 of its brief, that the Defence has been unable to test the organisation of the NLA due to the non-existence of any credible documentary evidence, is without merit. Your Honours, the NLA regulations that I just mentioned are reliable, are relevant, and have probative value. We have here the author Gzim Ostreni. We also had a brigade commander, Bushi, who implemented them. Also, Bezruchenko testified about the reliability of the regulations. The regulations of the NLA were produced from March until April and, exceptionally, early May 2001. Ostreni acknowledged the fact that he used as sources KLA documents, regulations, KPC, as well as regulations from the Republic of Albania and the former Yugoslavia. But, Your Honours, the Spanish civil code also used as a source the French civil code. Ostreni also acknowledged that not all the institutions, not all the structures which were foreseen in the regulations were implemented. He testified that the NLA was an army, an organised group in process of development, and they didn't expect that the war will end so soon. And, Your Honours, I will also call your attention to the fact that UCK translate from Albanian into English indistinctively NLA and KLA. Therefore, Your Honours, Tarculovski's argument in paragraphs 69 -- excuse me, 68 to 69 of his brief, that where he states that the NLA regulations are mere copies of the KLA and the KPC documents, is flawed. Your Honours, numerous internal international armed conflicts between states [indiscernible] armed groups have occurred. And, regretfully, IHL have not been respected; for example, the Americans and the Japanese in the Second World War, the Americans in Vietnam, the Apartheid regime, the Cuban internal conflict. These are some examples. Therefore, Boskoski's argument that the implementation of humanitarian standards is a key criteria to establish the existence of an organised armed group is without merit. This is in paragraph 263 of Boskoski's final brief. Nevertheless, Your Honour, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the NLA took measures to enforce the implementation of IHL. NLA documents and regulations foresaw -- will establish the respect of the international convention such as the Geneva Convention, as well as acknowledge the jurisdiction of the ICTY. I will refer Your Honours to Exhibit P487, page 4; Exhibit P507; as well as the rules of service of the NLA, which is Exhibit P498. The ERN range is R062-6775, page 6; as well as page 12 of the same documents. The NLA regulations also foresaw disciplinary measures which were to be implemented by the brigade and battalion commanders. I will refer Your Honours to the same rules of service of the NLA, Exhibit P498, ERN R062-6923, pages 4 to 6. Even for a certain period of time, Your Honour, the NLA had military police; but as Ostreni testified, they were integrated into the brigades. It was a reminiscence of the KLA, but this does not mean that the NLA didn't have personnel dealing with disciplinary measures. As Bushi testified, Xhavit Hasani, officer for morale and information, was the one dealing or talking to the detainees, to the NLA people arrested. Also, Your Honours, during the initial training of the new recruits, they were actually taught about the ordinary laws of war and international conventions, as well as their duty to respect civilians and civilian property. Your Honours, the NLA had the manpower, the resources, and the level of development to carry out concerted operations involving different brigades by June 2001. We saw that in the directive, Exhibit P487, exhibited by Gzim Ostreni. Nevertheless, the political context, meaning the cease-fire agreement, as well as the Ohrid Agreement, made the full implementation of the directive impossible. Nevertheless, Your Honour, the evidence presented in trial has proved that the NLA General Staff had the ability to determine a unified military strategy, as well as to plan and coordinate different brigades on the field who were operating in different fronts. Your Honours, I will refer to paragraph 29 of Exhibit P497, as well as Exhibit P499, page 7. Your Honours, the brigade commanders reported to the General Staff. The General Staff issue orders and instructions down to the chain of command, which the NLA members had the obligation to implement. I would refer Your Honours to the rules of service of the NLA, Exhibit P498, ERN R062-6774, page 13. Also, Your Honour, brigade commanders from different brigades who were sharing the same front, they indeed met and kept in contact in order to coordinate their operations. Your Honours, the progressive territorial advance, as well as the successful tactical operations of the NLA, could have only occur with a General Staff which was able to establish a unified military strategy, as well as to coordinate and plan the different brigades on the field. I will refer Your Honours to an assessment document, a research document drawn by NATO in 2003. It's Exhibit P493, pages 3 and 12. NATO defined the NLA as a well armed, well disciplined, and highly motivated organisation that enjoy majority support from within the area; and when referring to one brigade, appears to be a highly developed level of organisation and discipline which allows the brigade to function effectively. Therefore, Your Honours, Boskoski's argument in paragraph 263, stating that concerted operations involving different brigades is a key requirement to establish the existence of an organised armed group, is without merit. It may be relevant, Your Honours, but it is not a key or a determinative requirement. Your Honours, the NLA did carry out operations in different fronts simultaneously. For example, in June, the NLA was operating in Aracinovo and Tetovo. In August, Your Honours, the NLA were operating. In July and August they were basically operating in all the fronts at the same time. Early August, they were in Tetovo, Exhibit 1D229.1. They were in Aracinovo, Exhibit 2D39, page 3. They were in Radusa, Exhibits P605 and P609. And they also operated in Kumanovo, Exhibits 2D39, page 2, and 2D44, page 3. Even the UBK reports were reporting or informing about the operations that the NLA was carrying out in the different fronts. I will refer Your Honours to Exhibits 2D40, 2D44, 2D39. Therefore, Your Honours, Tarculovski argument that the NLA brigades were unable to operate in different fronts in different locations simultaneously is flawed. I will refer to paragraphs 59 to 60 to -- of Tarculovski's brief. Your Honours, the evidence at trial has shown that the NLA members had the obligation to carry out -- to wear uniforms when carrying out military operations. Nevertheless, as any other member of any other army when they were on leave, they would be wearing civilian clothing. Bolton, on page 1698, and Bouckaert, in page 3218, testified that every single time that they met with the NLA, they were wearing uniforms. According to Bolton in page 1699, if a NLA member was with a civilian, he will always had on his uniform, a distinctive sign that will identify him as a member of the NLA. On this matter, Your Honour, I will refer to the Prosecution's brief, paragraphs 471 to 472. Therefore, Your Honour, Tarculovski's submission on this point is unsound. Your Honours, Tarculovski has referred to this matter in paragraphs 82 to 92; and, indeed, his argument is not supported by the evidence cited in footnote 130. Your Honour, Ostreni was appointed by Ali Ahmeti as chief of the General Staff. He acted and he was regarded by NLA members such as Bushi, also by the international community and by the Macedonian authorities, as the Chief of Staff of the NLA. I will refer Your Honours to P93, page 34, that document produced by NATO, who refers to him as the Chief of Staff of the NLA. I will also refer to P485, page 3, a document produced by the minister of defence which also refers to him as the Chief of Staff of the NLA. Indeed, Bushi [sic] acted at the Chief of Staff. He issued instructions, he reported the orders issued from Ali Ahmeti, he received the reporting from the brigade commanders, he drafted the regulations, he even issued communiques, and he was the person dealing with the disbandment of the NLA. Thus, Your Honour, Tarculovski's submission in paragraph 111 is without merit. Ostreni, Your Honours, knew perfectly well and explained -- Your Honours, I have just been reminded that in page 69, line 5, it appears as "Bushi acted as the Chief of Staff." It should read, obviously, "Ostreni acted as the Chief of Staff." Ostreni knew and explained perfectly well where the headquarters of the General Staff were located. Initially, they were in Vejce, then they moved to Prizren Kosovo, and some elements of the General Staff were moving to Sipkovica. He testified about that in pages 7712 to 7714, and paragraph 32 of Exhibit P497. He knew and testified about the communications that he was using with the brigade commanders, phone and Internet. This is on pages 7749 to 7751. Your Honours, he also testified actually about the approximate number of casualties, 68. There is in 7749 to 7751. I would like to correct, actually, the reference with regards to the communication which was in page 7424. And, Your Honours, Gzim Ostreni may have not known exactly the structure of the NLA before March 2001, because he was abroad and he was the Chief of Staff of KPC in Kosovo. Therefore, Your Honour, Mr. Tarculovski's submissions in this regard in paragraph 64 are without merit. Your Honour, before moving to the third area, I would like to deal with three submissions raised by my learned colleagues. First, the required mens rea of the accused with regard to armed conflict, the mens rea of the perpetrators, and, finally, the relevance of state practice. With regards to mens rea of the accused, Your Honours, the Prosecution has to prove that the accused knew or had reason to know the factual circumstances of the conflict, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to determine whether these facts presented at trial are constitutive of an armed conflict. I will refer Your Honours to Naletilic appeals judgement, paragraphs 114 and 119. Your Honours, the Prosecution has proved that Johan Tarculovski, a police officer working as an escort of the president, knew or, in the alternative, had reason to know the factual circumstances in Macedonian of the conflict. He saw how his friends, his colleagues were killed in Ljubotenski Bacila. He even led an operation in Ljuboten where he said, "This is a state of war." Ljube Boskoski, Your Honour, the minister of the interior, he also knew or, in the alternative, had to know the factual circumstances underlying the armed conflict. Boskoski was issuing orders, he was issuing press releases concerning military activities, he was on the ground on a regular basis. Consequently, Your Honours, Boskoski's submission that the Prosecution has failed to establish that "Boskoski knew of the existence of an armed conflict and knew of the nature of that conflict as neither he nor the government officials never took the view that an armed conflict existed" is again without merit. I will refer Your Honours to paragraphs 458 to 470 of Mr. Boskoski's brief. Tarculovski raises a similar argument in paragraph 117 of his brief. Your Honour, I would like to draw your attention to footnote 959 in paragraph 467 of Boskoski's brief. In order to support this contention, Boskoski quotes his own memoire, Exhibit P402. The ERN range will be N000-9607, page 31. But if we read that page, Your Honours, we will see the prime minister, Ljubco Georgievski, wanted to declare the state of war. We will see how Boskoski himself acknowledge that he was working 24 hours, seven days per week because the military conflict was on top of his worries. Your Honours, the Prosecution does not have the obligation to exclude the possibility that Boskoski could have committed in good faith a mistake of fact or law with regard to the issue of armed conflict. The Prosecution merely has to prove that Ljube Boskoski either knew or had reason to know of the factual circumstances in Macedonia in 2001. It is up to the Trial Chamber to legally qualify this factual circumstances. By proving that the accused knew these factual circumstances, we are excluding this error of fact. And, Your Honours, with regards to the error of law, I will refer to Kordic appeal judgement, paragraphs 303 and 311, when the Appeals Chamber -- when the Appeals Chamber reiterated that the accused has to be aware of the factual circumstances basically. Therefore, Your Honours, Boskoski's argument in paragraph 471 of his brief is without merit. Your Honour, in those circumstances, when a subordinate of the accused commits a crime, the Prosecution has to prove that the accused either knew or had reason to know the victim's status; and I will refer Your Honours to Naletilic appeal judgement paragraph 114 footnote 257. Therefore, Tarculovski's argument that the accused needs to have only knowledge of the victims' status in paragraph 125 of his brief is without merit. Now, Your Honours, I will move to the mens rea of the perpetrator which has also been raised by my learned colleague Tarculovski in paragraph 129. In a similar circumstances, when a subordinate of the accused commits the crime, perpetrates a crime, the perpetrator must know or have reason to know also the victims' status; and the Prosecution refers to Halilovic trial judgement, paragraph 36, and Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraph 847, on this matter. Therefore, Your Honours, Tarculovski's submission in paragraph 124 that the mens rea standard of the perpetrator is merely being aware of the victims' status is flawed. Furthermore, no source has been cited to support this argument. And, finally, Your Honour, I just briefly mention an issue which had already been dealt by this Trial Chamber in your decision of the 27th of February, but has been raised again by both parties. Your Honours stated in such decision, in paragraph 6, that the existence of an armed conflict in Macedonia in 2001 is a question of fact and that public statement by states or organisations have no relevance for establishing the factual issue of armed conflict. Therefore, Your Honours, the arguments raised by the accused Tarculovski in paragraphs 112 to 116, and the accused Boskoski in paragraph 264 to 269, stating that the names that the countries and organisations gave to the NLA are a state practice that reflects the state of customary law are without merit. Your Honours, I would like to conclude the second part of my submissions stating that the Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the NLA was an organised armed group able to engage in an armed conflict. The NLA had a hierarchical structure with an effective and functioning chain of command, with the General Staff on top as the leadership, and the brigades and others subunits below. The brigade commanders were reporting to the General Staff, the General Staff were issuing orders and instructions, and the General Staff was able to actually define a unified military strategy and to coordinate and plan the brigade's military activities, and the NLA brigades were indeed able to carry out these operations in different fronts simultaneously. Your Honours, the General Staff was able to obtain weaponry, uniforms, equipment, mainly thanks to the funds coming from the diaspora. The NLA was issuing its own communiques, had to its own regulations. And the NLA was regarded by the international community as a valid negotiating partner, among other factors. And, Your Honours, the Macedonian conflict indeed caught the attention of the international community. I will simply refer to the UN Security Council Resolution, Exhibit 1D346, and on this particular point Your Honours, I will refer to paragraphs 491 to 498 of the Prosecution's final brief. And, finally, Your Honours, I will move to the third and last part of my submission, the intensity of the armed conflict. The armed conflict between the Macedonian security forces and the NLA started at least January 2001 and lasted -- that is, until September 2001. Therefore, there were clashes before and afterwards. Your Honours, you can find a detailed chronological description of the geographical development of the armed conflict in paragraphs 396 to 427 of the Prosecution brief. I won't deal with that matter now. I just want to highlight the fact that the NLA at some point had authority over the 20 per cent of the territory of Macedonia. Your Honours, an evidence of the intensity of the armed conflict was the weaponry that the Macedonian security forces had to use in order to face the NLA. They were using large-calibre artillery, multi-barrel rocket launchers, combat aircrafts, fixed-wing ground attack planes, and helicopter gunships, anti-aircraft guns, tanks, APCs, and at the beginning of the conflict, Your Honours, the army established tactical operational groups with the purpose to destroy the NLA in combat operations. With regards to the manpower of both parties, Your Honours, I will simply refer to paragraphs 465, 468 to 469 of the Prosecution's final brief. But, in a nutshell, the NLA had approximately 6.000 members, although some sources mention 8.000. The army employ per month 15.000 soldiers, and the police mobilised at the peak of the conflict around 10.200 reserve police officers, on top of the regular police officers. This high number of mobilised police officers indeed is an evidence of the seriousness of the conflict. The president, Your Honour, issue orders with the purpose of destroying the NLA and to regain the territorial control and the NLA authority. And also Boskoski, as the minister of the interior, established special police units; for example, the Lions, reactivated the posebna unit, special police unit that operated in complex situations when law and order were disrupted. Boskoski also restructure operation headquarters Ramno. He ordered the redeployment of the police to conflict areas. He mobilised and demobilised reservists, he set up check-points, and he even limited that citizens' movement in the main cities of the country, such as Kumanovo, Aracinovo, Tetovo, and Bitola. As a result, Your Honours, a large number of the Macedonian population had to flee the country. I will refer Your Honours to paragraph 428 of the Prosecution's brief, as there are many sources. The Macedonian sources, for example, mention that over 80.000 fled the country, and over 86.000 were internally displaced. In conclusion, Your Honours, the evidence presented at trial proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the NLA sufficiently had the characteristics of an organised armed group, which was engaged in an internal armed conflict with the Macedonian security forces during the relevant time-period of the indictment. Further, the intensity of the armed violence was of a scale that met the intensity prong of the Tadic case. Your Honours, I will end my submissions from a quote from Exhibit P464, which is a book written by three former members of the Macedonian army. In the ERN range N006-3325, page 2, the authors stated: "Macedonia waged a real seven-month war which followed the theory and practice of wars waged to date. The state authorities did not want to recognise or accept this situation - a state of war." At this point, Your Honours, I will be happy to answer your answers, or I will turn over to my colleague, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution's final comments today concern sentencing. In our final brief, we have addressed briefly the primary factors that we suggest should be taken into consideration, and those are the gravity of the offence and relevant aggravating factors. With respect to the gravity of the offence, this has been cited as the primary consideration in determining a sentence. I refer to the Celebici Appeal Judgement, paragraph 731. The Appeals Chamber in the same case also held that this consideration also applies in cases where responsibility is based solely on Article 7(3), and that can be found at paragraph 732 of the same judgement. The Prosecution has alleged, and we submit that we have proven beyond a reasonable doubt the charges set forth in the indictment. With regard to the accused Ljube Boskoski, it has been proven that he bears criminal responsibility for the failure to investigate or to punish the crimes set out in Counts 1, 2, and 3 of the indictment. By failing to investigate or to punish these crimes, the accused Boskoski has allowed seven murders, the wanton destruction of 14 homes, and the cruel treatment of at least 36 ethnic Albanian individuals to go unsolved. He has allowed the perpetrators of these crimes to escape accountability. He has allowed members of the Macedonian police - his subordinates - to rampage through a previously peaceful village, killing, beating and burning homes, with impunity. These crimes are grave in and of themselves, but we submit each more so when taking into account the impact they have had on such a small, close-knit community. The damage done, and the bewilderment as to how they came to be targeted, was clear in the testimony of the crime-base witnesses. In terms of aggravating factors, first and foremost must be Ljube Boskoski's abuse of his position of authority as the Macedonian minister of the interior at the time of these crimes. Both the Hadzihasanovic appeals judgement at paragraph 320, and the Seromba appeals judgement at paragraph 230 cite this as an aggravating factor. Your Honours, the evidence has shown that this is a case of real abuse of power. As set out by my colleague Mr. Saxon, from the outset Mr. Boskoski set out to "prove the opposite," to use the words of his advisor, Sofija Galeva-Petrovska. And that is at transcript page 8806. As early as the 14th of August, Mr. Boskoski was stating to the media that all that remained was to establish whether the, to use his words, "five terrorists" were "from Ljuboten itself, or whether those terrorists were also imported." And this is in Exhibit P362. As Mr. Saxon has described, this intent to prove the opposite guided Mr. Boskoski in whatever steps he took following the attack on Ljuboten. His failure to ensure a competent investigation was carried out, his failure to punish the perpetrators, and his ongoing justification and rationalisation of the crimes that took place in Ljuboten amounts to a serious abuse of his authority and a serious breach of the public trust. In Naletilic, the Trial Chamber held that Naletilic's failure to punish the soldiers conveyed the message that their behaviour was tolerable. And that can be found at paragraph 28 of the Trial Chamber judgement. The Prosecution submits that a similar situation arises here. The accused Boskoski's failure to hold accountable the people who perpetrated these crimes sent the message that this unlawful conduct would be tolerated by his words. By his actions and by his inactions, Ljube Boskoski helped to create a culture of impunity within the Ministry of Interior. He used his position of authority to shield his subordinates from liability, and to paint those who raised their concerns about these crimes as enemies of Macedonia. This abuse of his power is an aggravating factor that the Prosecution submits the Court should take into account. A further aggravating circumstance is the particular vulnerability of many of the victims, and this factor is cited in the Aleksovski trial judgement at paragraph. In this case, many of the cruel treatment victims were viciously beaten while unarmed and defenceless and in police custody. Many of these victims were already seriously injured and physically incapable of defending themselves, yet the police continued to beat them in various police stations around Skopje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the Prosecutor to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the most seriously injured, those who were sent to Skopje City Hospital continued to be beaten by the police. Your Honours, we submit that this is it also an aggravating factor which should be reflected in the sentence. Finally, Your Honours, Mr. Boskoski's clear lack of remorse or sympathy of any kind for the victims deserves consideration by the Trial Chamber. What is disturbing is that, in the many statements Mr. Boskoski has given to the media, not once is there any recognition that innocent civilians may have suffered as a result of the deaths, beatings, and destruction that the villagers of Ljuboten endured. This lack of remorse or lack of any recognise nation the ethnic Albanian residents of Ljuboten have suffered at all is clear in Boskoski's own words. Although this has already been quoted today, it does deserve further consideration, and I refer to the quote from his memoirs where he states: "The political Court in The Hague is a brilliant invention which has nothing do with human rights at all. Why? Because it is being used to incriminate the Macedonian security forces for alleged crimes in Ljuboten, where the security forces of Macedonia actually saved Ljuboten." That is Exhibit P402, ERN N000-9704 to N000-9711 at page 6. These memoirs were published in 2004. So even three years after the crimes in Ljuboten, with all the information that was clear at this point, there's no acknowledgment of any suffering or pain caused by the attack on the village. In fact, according to Mr. Boskoski, it was the police who were the victims and the villagers are actually the beneficiaries of this attack. Your Honours, this clear lack of remorse or sympathy should be certainly be considered as an aggravating factor for the purposes of sentencing. Finally, with regards to Mr. Boskoski, it is an established principle that the Trial Chamber must take into account the general practice regarding sentencing and the domestic jurisdiction, although this is not binding. I refer to the Hadzihasanovic trial judgement at paragraph 2074. While the domestic law of Macedonia provides no guidance for responsibility based on failure to punish, Article 404 of the Macedonia Criminal Code does cover war crimes, including the offences charged in this indictment. It calls for a minimum sentence of ten years imprisonment up to a maximum of life. Taking this into account, along with the gravity of the underlying crimes, and the aggravating factors that the Prosecution has set out, it is our respectful submission that the accused Boskoski is guilty of the crimes that we have alleged in the indictment and that a sentence of 12 years imprisonment would be appropriate. With regards to the accused Johan Tarculovski, I have already set out the gravity of the crimes, so I won't repeat that at this point. In respect of aggravating features, we submit that his direct participation and his presence during the commission of the crimes in Ljuboten is an aggravating factor the Trial Chamber is entitled to consider. We rely on the Banovic sentencing judgement at paragraph 43 in support of this proposition. Again, the vulnerability of the victims is a further aggravating circumstance, at least in regards to the cruel treatment of the victims at Ametovski house Brace's house. These men were unarmed, detained, and utterly incapable of defending themselves. The Trial Chamber in Celebici has also stated that a sadistic or cruel motivation behind the crimes is another aggravating circumstance that can be taken into account. That is at paragraph 1268 of that judgement. Your Honours, the evidence proves that such a motivation was exhibited in this case. The words and above all the actions of the police, while beating the detainees in Ljuboten, clearly demonstrates this. At this point, I would ask that Exhibit P195 be shown. Your Honours, what we see here is a photograph showing a large cross that was carved into the back of the one of the cruel treatment victims at Ametovski house. I would ask now that Exhibit P14 be shown. Your Honours, this shows Atulla Qaili, a victim of cruel treatment in Ljuboten, who, as we heard earlier, arrived at Brace's house already looking like he was going to die. Thank you. That can be taken off now. Thank you. Your Honours, these pictures graphically demonstrate the sadistic cruel motivation behind the crimes the police, led by the accused Tarculovski, committed on 12 August, 2001. This, we submit, is a proper aggravating factor for the Trial Chamber to consider. Furthermore, like the accused Boskoski, Johan Tarculovski has also failed to show any awareness or any sort of remorse for the suffering that may have been caused by his actions; and as with accused Ljube Boskoski, I turn to the accused Tarculovski's own words, or at least the words of his counsel. I refer to paragraph 395 of Tarculovski's final brief, where it states: "Mr. Tarculovski, himself, is not aware that he had person operated any crime, nor caused suffer to go anyone." Again, Your Honours, what is demonstrated is a total lack of awareness or any remorse for his actions and the undoubted suffering that these actions caused. Your Honour, this is a further aggravating factor we invite the Trial Chamber to consider. As I have already mentioned, for the crimes the accused Tarculovski has been charged with, the Macedonian Criminal Code calls for a minimum sentence of ten years imprisonment. In light of the gravity of the offences and the aggravating circumstances, the Prosecution submits that this is a case that is deserving of a substantially longer sentence than the minimum provided for by Macedonia law. And with respect, Your Honours, we submit that a sentence of 15 years imprisonment would be appropriate in this case. And, Your Honours, that concludes the Prosecution's submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn, and thank you, Mr. Saxon, and all the members of your team, for the assistance that has been given today. We now adjourn. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning to continue the submissions.
